power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Supporting Early Career Development Through Volitional Personality Change: A Multi-Layered Evaluation of a Digital Intervention

text.text: Personality change interventions (PCIs) offer promising opportunities for personal development, yet little is known about how different psychological layers of personalitythoughts, feelings, behaviors, skills, and identity-respond to intentional change efforts.
This study addressed that question through a six-week smartphone-based intervention tailored to students' preparation for entering the workforce, an applied setting in which PCIs remain understudied.

Final-year undergraduate clinical psychology students (N = 565) participated in one of three interventions designed to enhance resilience, social boldness, or punctuality, with a quasi-experimental control group for comparison (N = 99).

Participants in all three conditions showed meaningful growth in the targeted facet, with gains exceeding changes in non-targeted facets, surpassing those observed in the control group, and persisting at the fourweek follow-up.
Moreover, perceived feasibility of change moderated intervention effectiveness.

Finally, participants targeting resilience and social boldness showed significant growth across psychological layers, whereas those targeting punctuality changed primarily in the behavioral and skill layers.
The identity layer-representing how participants see themselves-exhibited the smallest degree of change.

Collectively, these findings enrich volitional personality change (VPC) theory by illuminating how personality change unfolds across different psychological layers, while also demonstrating the feasibility of PCIs in supporting the school-to-work transition.

Transitioning from higher education to the labor market poses a dual challenge for students: they must acquire not only job-relevant knowledge, but also the personal competencies needed to navigate career demands (Blokker et al., 2023).

The question of whether personality is fixed or amenable to change has long stood at the heart of personality psychology.
Although traits show strong rank-order stability, there is also ample evidence that personality is malleable.

By adopting a deliberate, multi-layered approach to evaluating PCI effectiveness, this study seeks to provide a more nuanced understanding of which personality layers are most responsive to intervention.
Through a six-week smartphone-based PCI tailored to the professional preparation context, this study took a novel approach to disentangling how different psychological layers respond to intervention.

Specifically, we examined VPC in final-year undergraduate psychology students preparing for their first clinical internship through a career preparation course that incorporated career exploration activities and a brief internship.
Participants selected one of three personality facets-social boldness, punctuality, or resilience-as their personal development targets.
These facets were derived from thematic analyses of focus group discussions with subgroups of course instructors, mentors, and former students and reflected recurring internship-related challenges.
Participants were assessed at four time points: pre-intervention, mid-intervention, post-intervention, and after four weeks.
A control group was also assessed repeatedly over a comparable timeframe.
The intervention was delivered via smartphone, consistent with a growing body of research using digital tools for non-clinical interventions (e.g., Stieger et al., 2021).

text.text: This format enabled flexible delivery in daily life while supporting scalable, cost-efficient implementation and continuous assessment.
The study had three primary goals.
First, we examined whether desired changes occurred within the intervention group.

In line with existing evidence, we hypothesized that participants would show increases in their targeted facet from pre-to post-intervention (Hypothesis 1) and that these gains would persist at the four-week follow-up (Hypothesis 2).

To further evaluate the robustness of pre-post intervention effects, we examined changes in targeted versus non-targeted facets within the intervention group and compared changes in the intervention group with those observed in a control group.
We expected larger increases in targeted than non-targeted facets (Hypothesis 3), and larger increases than those observed for the corresponding facet in the control group (Hypothesis 4).
Second, we explored potential moderators of pre-to post-intervention changes.

Several frameworks of VPC have proposed determinants of successful change, some of which have received preliminary empirical support, although the evidence remains limited and inconsistent (e.g., Allemand & Flückiger, 2017; Haehner et al., 2024; Hennecke et al., 2014).

text.text: Among the determinants most recurrently highlighted are engagement in the change process, motivation to change, and beliefs about the attainability of change.
Drawing on these theoretical and empirical insights, we examined four moderators: intervention engagement, desire to change, perceived value of change, and perceived feasibility of change.

Specifically, we expected greater intervention engagement to be associated with larger increases in the targeted facet (Hypothesis 5a), consistent with evidence that greater investment in change efforts facilitates goal attainment and personality development (Hudson et al., 2019; Stieger et al., 2021).

Finally, we hypothesized that perceived feasibility of change (Hypothesis 5d)-the belief that change is attainable-would positively predict increases in the targeted facet (Hennecke et al., 2014).

text.text: Given that these moderators are conceptually related, they were examined simultaneously to assess their unique contributions to intervention effectiveness.
The final and third goal of the study was to investigate whether different psychological layers of personality vary in their rate of change.
Given the exploratory nature of this question, we did not formulate any a priori hypotheses.

In addition to the traditional layers of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors-components central to trait theories of personality (Allport, 1961)-we included two dimensions closely related to personality but not typically distinguished as core components; namely identity and skills.

While trait theories focus on patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving, other perspectives emphasize the role of identity in personality functioning and development, capturing how individuals perceive and interpret themselves (McAdams et al., 2021).

text.text: Identity is particularly relevant to VPC because development goals are argued to emerge from discrepancies between actual and desired selves (Hennecke et al., 2014), and because incorporating behavioral, affective, and cognitive changes into one's self-concept (i.e., assimilation) may help sustain long-term personality change (Jackson & Wright, 2024).

text.text: By including identity as an additional outcome, we examined whether PCIs influence not only what individuals think, feel, and do, but also how they see themselves.
Finally, our investigation incorporated a skill layer.

Whereas traits reflect typical patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behavior across situations (i.e., tendencies), skills reflect the capacity to enact specific behaviors when needed (i.e., capacities) and are generally considered to be more malleable (Soto et al., 2022).

text.text: Because PCIs often employ strategies similar to-but more extensive and sustained than-those used in skill training, such interventions may foster growth in soft skills alongside personality change.
Practically, these findings may inform scalable, digitally delivered PCIs that support students in preparing for occupational roles and guide PCI efforts in workplace settings.

At the beginning of the semester, participants in the intervention group received verbal information about the intervention and study and were invited to provide consent for their data to be used in research.
To encourage honest reporting, participants were informed that their grades would be based solely on participation, not on the content of their responses.
Interventions were timed to coincide with students' internships, facilitating application of intervention activities in practice.
Participants selected one of three targets-social boldness (57%, N = 321), punctuality (16%, N = 93), or resilience (26%, N = 151)-based on their personal development goals.

All three personality facets were measured in every participant at four consecutive time points: shortly before the intervention (pretest, T1), mid-way after three weeks (T2), immediately following the intervention (post-test, T3), and four weeks after the intervention (follow-up, T4).
As a result, participants who focused on one target also served as a comparison group for those focusing on alternative targets.
In addition to these within-intervention comparisons, a parallel control group was recruited concurrently and completed the same measures without participating in the intervention.
The intervention was delivered to final-year undergraduate students in clinical psychology at XXX (institution blinded for review) as part of a career preparation course.
This course prepares students for professional practice through career exploration sessions, a brief internship, and other related activities.
Participation was incentivized through higher course grades but was not required to pass the course.
The sample was collected across two waves and consisted of 565 students at pre-intervention, of whom 541 participated at midintervention, 552 at post-intervention, and 275 at follow-up 1 .
The majority of students (86%; N = 487) participated in all six intervention weeks.
An additional 12% (N = 68) completed five weeks, and only 2% (N = 10) completed four weeks, consistent with the course-credit requirement that allowed missing at most one week.
Participants were predominantly women (87%), with an average age of 21.64 years (range = 18-55 years).
A control group was recruited through convenience sampling among psychology students at various stages of their academic programs.
Initially, 99 participants completed the pre-intervention assessment, with 91 participating at mid-intervention, and 78 at postintervention.
Most participants were women (91%), and the average age was 22.28 years (ranging from 18 to 51 years).
The demographic composition of the control group-in terms of gender and age-was thus broadly comparable to that of the intervention group.

text.text: Each Monday, participants received a notification to complete the weekly intervention.
Nonresponders received up to two daily reminders until completion or until the session closed on Wednesday.
Each week began with two app-based microinterventions, varying across weeks.

Examples included psychoeducational videos to foster knowledge about personality change or reflection exercises such as cognitive restructuring exercises, guiding participants to identify, evaluate, and modify their thought patterns.
Upon completing these micro-interventions, participants received a behavioral activation task designed to promote behaviors relevant to their targeted personality facet.
Participants ranked six behavioral activation tasks from easiest to most challenging during the first week, creating a personalized hierarchy to gradually increase task difficulty.

Each week, participants were instructed to translate the behavioral activation task into an implementation intention-a concrete if-then plan tailored to the professional preparation context participants were likely to encounter that week.
Each subsequent Monday, students completed a brief assessment of their experiences before proceeding to the next intervention module.
Social boldness, punctuality, and resilience were assessed at all measurement occasions using a multi-layered, contextualized instrument developed through a four-step process.
First, operational definitions of each facet were formulated in collaboration with course instructors to ensure relevance to the professional preparation context.

Second, items were drawn from conceptually related scales in the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP; Goldberg et al., 2006) and the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; Soto et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, items were drawn from conceptually related scales in the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP; <ref type="bibr">Goldberg et al., 2006)</ref> and the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI; <ref type="bibr">Soto et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, items were classified according to the psychological layer they reflected (i.e., thoughts, feelings, behaviors, skills, or identity).
Finally, items were selected, adapted, or newly developed to ensure balanced representation of each layer while maintaining conceptual overlap across layers.
Further details regarding measure development are provided in the supplemental materials (Supplementary Method S1).
Phrasing was standardized to reflect each psychological layer consistently.
Feelings items referred to emotions (e.g., "I feel confident sharing my opinion" for social boldness).
Thoughts items were phrased to indicate beliefs or convictions (e.g., "I believe that planning is the key to good results" for punctuality).
Behavior items explicitly referred to actions (e.g., "I give up quickly after a setback" for resilience).
Identity items began with "I am" (e.g., "I am a procrastinator" for punctuality).
Skill items were phrased using "I can" or "I am bad at" (e.g., "I am bad at expressing my opinion" for social boldness).
All items were rated on a 5point scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree).
The full item set and instructions are provided in the supplemental material (Supplementary Method S2).
Cronbach's alpha values at T1 indicated good reliability for 12 of the 15 scales (Kline, 1999), ranging from α = .70 (resilience -behavior) to α = .91 (social boldness -identity).

Composite facet scores were calculated by averaging items across psychological layers.
At T1, participants rated their desire to change their targeted personality facet using the item: "On a scale of 1 to 10, how much [facet] do you want to develop compared to how you are right now?"
(1 = a little more;10 = very much more).
At T1, participants rated how feasible they perceived their development goal using the item: "On a scale of 1 to 10, how difficult does this development goal seem to you?"
(1 = very easy;10 = very difficult).
At T1, respondents reported their perceived value of change using the item: "On a scale of 1 to 10, how important is it to you to reach this development goal?"
(1 = slightly important;10 = extremely important).
Engagement was assessed for both reflection exercises and behavioral activation tasks.
Following each reflection-based exercise, participants rated the depth of their reflection on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (I barely thought about it) to 5 (I thought about it very deeply).
Behavioral engagement was assessed through self-reported completion of weekly behavioral activation tasks and, when applicable, completion of activities involving participants' chosen change team.
Reflection and behavioral engagement scores were aggregated across the intervention period and modeled as indicators of a latent intervention engagement factor.
Factor scores extracted from this model were used in subsequent analyses.
The full measure development procedure is described in the Supplementary Materials (Supplementary Method S3).
All research questions were examined using a series of linear longitudinal multilevel models (MLMs) in RStudio (version 4.4.2; R Core Team, 2023).
MLMs were used to account for the nested structure of the data, with repeated measurements over time (Level 1: Time) nested within participants (Level 2: Person).

For Hypotheses 1 and 2 concerning the degree of change and maintenance at follow-up, all four measurement occasions were included (i.e., pre-intervention, mid-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up).
Time was coded in weeks to reflect the unequal spacing between assessments (i.e., 3, 3, and 4 weeks, respectively).
In these models, estimated slopes (b) represent unstandardized change per week.
All other analyses focused on pre-to post-intervention change and therefore included only the first three measurement occasions.
In these models, time was coded as 0, 1, and 2, such that slopes (b) represent unstandardized change per time step of 3 weeks.
To facilitate interpretation, we additionally report standardized effect sizes (Cohen's d), calculated from observed scores, for the key effects in the main text 2 .
All models included random intercepts and slopes to account for individual differences in baseline scores and rates of change over time.

Our findings revealed significant increases in targeted resilience (d = .82), social boldness (d = .62), and punctuality (d = .22) over the course of the six-week intervention.

Whereas the effect for punctuality was comparable to the average effect reported in metaanalytic research on PCIs (d = .22), the effects for resilience and social boldness were substantially larger and approached the upper range of those observed in previous studies.

One possible explanation for these relatively large effects is that our intervention targeted rather narrow personality facets, which may be more amenable to intervention than broad trait domains (e.g., Allemand & Flückiger, 2017; Stieger et al., 2020).

text.text: A second explanation may be the intervention's contextual specificity: both change efforts and outcome assessments were centered on students' preparation for the school-to-work transition.
Such context-specific changes may be more readily achieved over a short period than broader personality changes that require generalization across multiple life domains (Jackson & Wright, 2024).

text.text: Importantly, because the meta-analytic benchmarks used for comparison (Haehner et al., 2024) are largely based on similar young adult samples, the relatively large effect sizes observed here are unlikely to reflect age-related personality plasticity alone.

text.text: Several findings lend further support to the intervention's effectiveness.
Improvements were stronger for targeted than non-targeted facets (d = .35) and changes in the intervention group exceeded those observed in the quasi-experimental control group (d = .43, on average).

Notably, small improvements in non-targeted facets within the intervention group did not differ significantly from corresponding changes in the control group, suggesting that they likely reflect normative changes (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2022) rather than secondary effects of the intervention.

text.text: Finally, consistent with both our expectations and previous research (e.g., Stieger et al., 2023), intervention gains were maintained at the four-week follow-up, with even further increases observed for social boldness (d = .19) and resilience (d = .09).

text.text: A second goal of the study was to examine potential moderators of intervention effectiveness, as prior work has yielded limited and inconsistent empirical support (e.g., Haehner et al., 2024; Jackson & Wright, 2024).

text.text: When all moderators were examined simultaneously, perceived feasibility of change emerged as a small but statistically significant predictor of greater increases in targeted facets over time.

This finding is consistent with theoretical models of VPC, which propose that individuals are more likely to initiate and sustain change efforts when they perceive change as attainable (Hennecke et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with theoretical models of VPC, which propose that individuals are more likely to initiate and sustain change efforts when they perceive change as attainable <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hennecke et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although this finding appears inconsistent with previous studies reporting weak or nonsignificant effects of beliefs about personality malleability (e.g., Hudson et al., 2021; Olaru et al., 2025), those studies assessed general beliefs about whether personality can change, whereas our measure captured the perceived difficulty of achieving a specific development goal and may therefore be more closely linked to sustained change efforts.

text.text: From a practical standpoint, these findings suggest that interventions may be more effective when they foster perceived feasibility, for example through psychoeducation and progress feedback that reinforce individuals' confidence in their ability to achieve their change goals.
Because the four moderators were conceptually related, they were examined simultaneously to estimate their unique contributions to personality change.

As some moderators may operate through one another (Olaru et al., 2025), the present estimates reflect unique rather than total effects and may therefore be smaller than those reported in studies examining moderators in isolation.

text.text: However, supplementary analyses examining each moderator separately produced the same overall pattern of results, suggesting that the null findings for intervention engagement, desire to change, and perceived value of change cannot be attributed solely to their simultaneous inclusion in the model.
In addition, measurement considerations may provide context for the null findings.

For example, because desire to change was assessed after participants selected a goal, it reflected goal strength rather than goal adoption, potentially reducing its predictive value compared with measures that also capture the absence of a change goal or desires in the opposite direction (Olaru et al., 2025).

text.text: Intervention engagement also failed to predict change, despite previous findings suggesting a positive association with personality growth (Hudson et al., 2019; Olaru et al., 2025).

text.text: One explanation may be the reliance on self-reported and retrospective engagement measures.
Future research could use more objective assessments, such as coded written reflections or experience-sampling measures of implementation enactment.
Beyond frequency of engagement, qualitative aspects of intervention participation may also matter.
Recent evidence suggests that the experienced valence of implementation attempts may be associated with stronger personality change (Olaru et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent evidence suggests that the experienced valence of implementation attempts may be associated with stronger personality change <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Olaru et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Different forms of engagement may also facilitate change at different psychological layers.

Although the present study was not designed to test these differential pathways, future research could examine whether specific intervention components (e.g., reflection) preferentially facilitate change at particular psychological layers (e.g., thoughts and feelings).

Finally, this study addressed a fundamental yet underexplored question in VPC research: which psychological layers of personality-thoughts, feelings, behaviors-are most responsive to intervention. Olaru et al. (2022) recently argued that personality scales in intervention research should be more balanced in terms of these layers, as many widely used measures emphasize certain layers unevenly across traits (Wilt & Revelle, 2015).

(2022)</ref> recently argued that personality scales in intervention research should be more balanced in terms of these layers, as many widely used measures emphasize certain layers unevenly across traits <ref type="bibr">(Wilt & Revelle, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The issue is that such imbalances can make it difficult to determine whether observed differences in change across personality domains reflect true differences in trait malleability or differences in the malleability of the layers assessed.
Building further on this call, the present study explicitly distinguished between different layers within each facet.
Findings for social boldness and resilience indicated that the intervention produced change in all three traditional personality layers of behavior, thoughts, and feelings.
In addition, the skill layer increased significantly, suggesting that the intervention also strengthened participants' capacities to perform behaviors when needed.

This is consistent with expectations, as social, emotional, and behavioral skills are considered particularly amenable to development and are often targeted using similar intervention strategies (Soto et al., 2022 (Soto et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: This is consistent with expectations, as social, emotional, and behavioral skills are considered particularly amenable to development and are often targeted using similar intervention strategies <ref type="bibr">(Soto et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Soto et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Identity also showed significant growth, reflecting that participants partially assimilated the changes into how they perceive themselves in professional contexts.
However, a different pattern emerged for punctuality, with significant increases in the skill and behavior layers but not in the thought, feeling, and identity layers.
This suggests that participants became more capable of being punctual and engaging in punctual behavior without corresponding changes in how they thought, felt, or perceived themselves.

It is possible that-despite our efforts to develop a balanced measure of punctuality including indicators for each psychological layer-traits may nevertheless differ in the extent to which they comprise affective, behavioral, cognitive, skill-related, and identity-based processes (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2026).

text.text: From this perspective, punctuality may be less strongly grounded in recurrent patterns of thoughts and feelings than social boldness or resilience.
When examining differences in rates of change across layers within social boldness and resilience, a broadly consistent pattern emerged.
In both facets, identity was among the slowest-changing layers, exhibiting significantly smaller increases than the two other layers.

These patterns suggest that identity may be particularly resistant to short-term interventioninduced change, which aligns with theoretical models proposing that it develops through a gradual reflective process in which new thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are slowly recognized and integrated into one's self-concept (Jackson & Wright, 2024).

text.text: This study has several limitations that point to promising avenues for future research.

First, the quasi-experimental design enhances internal validity relative to correlational designs without a control group (e.g., Hudson et al., 2019), but does not provide the full rigor of randomization.
text.formatted: First, the quasi-experimental design enhances internal validity relative to correlational designs without a control group (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hudson et al., 2019)</ref>, but does not provide the full rigor of randomization.

text.text: Specifically, self-selection into development goals resulted in baseline differences between the intervention and control groups, with intervention participants scoring lower on their targeted facet at baseline than control participants.
Although the MLMs controlled for such baseline differences, regression-to-the-mean effects cannot be ruled out entirely.

However, because self-selection into development goals is fundamental to VPC research, future research should retain it while using stronger controls, such as randomized wait-list designs that assign participants with similar development goals to immediate or delayed intervention groups (Haehner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, because self-selection into development goals is fundamental to VPC research, future research should retain it while using stronger controls, such as randomized wait-list designs that assign participants with similar development goals to immediate or delayed intervention groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Haehner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A second, related limitation of the present study concerns the potential influence of demand effects in the intervention condition, despite the inclusion of a control group.
That is, placebo effects may have influenced participants' personality ratings, with expectations potentially shaping perceived rather than actual change.
To mitigate demand effects, Hudson et al. (2019) have suggested using placebo tasks in the control group, but participants may notice that these tasks are unrelated to their development goals.
Another alternative is to use measures beyond self-report.

For example, informant reports may reduce self-serving bias and, although they can still be influenced by demand effects if informants are aware of the intervention's goals, this influence is typically less pronounced (e.g., Stieger et al., 2020 Stieger et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: For example, informant reports may reduce self-serving bias and, although they can still be influenced by demand effects if informants are aware of the intervention's goals, this influence is typically less pronounced (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Stieger et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Stieger et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: However, the observability of different psychological layers should also be considered, as self-observer agreement is typically stronger for overt aspects such as behavior than for more internal aspects such as thoughts (Wiedenroth et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, the observability of different psychological layers should also be considered, as self-observer agreement is typically stronger for overt aspects such as behavior than for more internal aspects such as thoughts <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wiedenroth et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, longer-term follow-up assessments could help mitigate concerns about demand effects, as such influences may naturally diminish over time.
Third, it remains unclear whether the observed personality changes lead to measurable improvements in participants' professional functioning.
While prior research has linked personality change to positive outcomes across life domains (e.g., Wright & Jackson, 2023), our study did not assess these outcomes.
text.formatted: While prior research has linked personality change to positive outcomes across life domains (e.g., Wright & Jackson, 2023), our study did not assess these outcomes.

text.text: Future research should incorporate criterion measures-such as work performance or satisfaction-to determine whether personality change translates into meaningful gains in professional preparation settings.
A final limitation concerns the specificity of our sample.

Participants were psychology students enrolled in the same course and were predominantly female, reflecting a broader trend in VPC research, which often relies on female-dominated psychology student samples (Haehner et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Participants were psychology students enrolled in the same course and were predominantly female, reflecting a broader trend in VPC research, which often relies on female-dominated psychology student samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Haehner et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although this homogeneity supports internal validity, it may limit generalizability and may have increased receptivity to reflective intervention components.
Moreover, despite completing short-term internships, participants had relatively limited exposure to professional settings.

Future research should extend this work to students in longer internships and to working populations, who are typically older and may exhibit more limited personality plasticity (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Future research should extend this work to students in longer internships and to working populations, who are typically older and may exhibit more limited personality plasticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This study provides initial evidence that PCIs can be effectively implemented in professional preparation settings, producing meaningful improvements in resilience and social boldness and, to a lesser extent, in punctuality over a six-week period.
Importantly, these effects were sustained at the six-week follow-up.
Moreover, our multi-layered approach contributes to theory by offering a more nuanced framework for understanding what aspects of personality interventions ultimately change.
Future research should replicate these findings in more diverse and professionally embedded samples to strengthen generalizability and assess longer-term impact.

Ultimately, we believe this study offers a promising path toward facilitating professional development, both by preparing students for their future careers and by fostering meaningful change in employees within organizations.

Participants reflect on a role model in their professional environment who embodies the desired level of their targeted personality facet, and describe how this person's behaviors, thoughts, and feelings tend to differ from their own.
They then recall a concrete professional situation in which they needed their targeted personality facet, and re-imagine how their role model would have thought, felt, and acted in that situation.
Participants identify two trusted individuals (friends, family, colleagues, or fellow students) to form their personal "change team" throughout the intervention.
Participants record the names of these two individuals in the app, and are encouraged to contact them immediately or later in the week at their convenience.
Participants receive a behavioral activation task tailored to the hierarchy of difficulty they selected in Week 1.
Example tasks by facet: • Social boldness: "Share your opinion or ideas in person with someone.

For instance, share your thoughts with a fellow student during a seminar or lecture, or offer a suggestion for improvement at your student job or internship" • Punctuality: "Arrive at least 10 minutes early at your student job, internship, lecture, or practical session.
This means planning your travel time and route well in advance.
Also, start your preparations on time (e.g., getting ready, gathering your materials) so that you can leave at your planned departure time" • Resilience: "Do something outside your comfort zone.
For a group project, take on a task you would normally pass on.
Or attend an event (e.g., organized by the student association) that you would usually avoid.
If you usually study at home, try doing it in a new location you haven't been to before"
Participants are instructed to create an 'if-then' plan to make the week's task concrete.
In this plan, they are asked to link a specific situation (the 'if') with a concrete action (the 'then').

Social boldness, punctuality, and resilience were assessed at all four measurement occasions using a multi-layered, contextualized instrument developed through a four-step process.

In the first step, the principal researchers and course instructors collaboratively formulated operational definitions for each facet, reflecting their meaning within the applied context of the course.

Social boldness was defined as the extent to which individuals confidently and effectively express their opinions and questions, stand up for their viewpoints, and comfortably engage in new or unfamiliar social interactions.

Punctuality describes the extent to which individuals create and follow plans, begin tasks on time, prepare thoroughly, meet deadlines and instructions, and value fulfilling their commitments and promises.

Resilience refers to the extent to which individuals respond to feedback, criticism, setbacks, or stressful situations, including both their immediate reactions and their ability to adapt, learn, and find solutions in response to these challenges.

Yet, surprisingly little research has examined whether interventions actually produce trait change across these different layers.
To date, psychological layers have primarily been examined as focal points of intervention design (Haehner et al., 2025) or theorized mechanisms of personality change (Bleidorn et al., 2026).
However, much less attention has been devoted to examining these layers as outcomes of PCIs.

Change is usually assessed at the level of domains or facets-and, in rare cases, at the level of personality nuances (Olaru et al., 2022)-using established trait inventories, such as the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2; Soto & John, 2017).

text.text: This approach introduces two key limitations.

First, many widely used Big Five item sets provide uneven coverage across psychological layers, disproportionately reflecting certain components (e.g., conscientiousness items primarily capture behavior, emotional stability items largely assess affect; Wilt & Revelle, 2015), which may skew interpretations of what exactly has changed perspective, this work sought to contribute to VPC literature by applying existing frameworks of VPC to the professional preparation context and offering nuanced insight into how personality change unfolds across different psychological layers.
